summary: Describes the Handle System namespace and service in detail. The namespace definition specifies handle syntax and semantic structure, and the data model defines data structures the protocol uses. It also covers service and operation models. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3651 describes the Handle System, a naming service for Internet resources. A handle is a name made of an authority part and a local part, and each handle holds a set of typed values with rules about who may read or change them. The document also explains how the service is arranged, with one global registry above many local services, and how a client looks up a handle and proves who it is.

questions: handle system namespace and service definition
subtitle: How the Handle System names Internet resources and where those names are kept

tldr.problem: The Handle System was designed as a general-purpose global name service for Internet resources, and its rules for how a handle is written, what a handle may point at, and who may change it were spread across several documents.
tldr.mechanism: This document gives the namespace (a handle is a naming authority and a local name separated by a slash), the data model (a set of typed values with permissions, a time to live and a timestamp), the service model (one Global Handle Registry above many Local Handle Services) and the operation model (resolution by referral and a challenge-response authentication protocol).
tldr.outcome: It is the reference for the rest of the Handle System documentation: the protocol byte layout is in RFC 3652 and the architectural overview in RFC 3650.

facts.label: Handle separator
facts.value: The ASCII character / between the naming authority and the local name

facts.label: Reserved naming authorities
facts.value: 0.NA for naming authorities, 0.TYPE for data types, 0.SERV for service handles

today: RFC 3651 is an Informational memo published in November 2003, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the service definition for the Handle System: the architectural overview is in RFC 3650 and the message formats are in RFC 3652.

sections.title: What the Handle System Does
sections.content:
The Handle System manages handles as globally unique names for Internet resources. It was originally conceived and described in a paper by Robert Kahn and Robert Wilensky in 1995, and it provides a general-purpose global name service that allows handles to be resolved and administrated securely over the public Internet.

The service comes in two categories. The handle resolution service turns a handle into its values, which is what clients use to find the resource a handle names. The handle administration service deals with client requests to manage those handles, including adding and deleting handles and updating handle values.

This document is the detailed description of the namespace, the data model, the service model and the operation model. The namespace definition specifies the handle syntax and its semantic structure. The data model defines the data structures used by the Handle System protocol and the pre-defined data types for carrying out the handle service. The service model defines the components and explains how they work together over the network. The operation model describes the service in terms of the messages exchanged between client and server, and the client authentication process. The architectural overview and the relationship to other Internet services such as DNS and LDAP are in the Handle System Overview, and the exact byte layout of each message is in the Handle System Protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The Handle System gives Internet resources a globally unique name and keeps the information attached to that name. This document is the reference for the whole system: what a handle looks like, what a handle holds, who runs the service and how a client talks to it.

sections.title: Handle Syntax and Naming Authorities
sections.content:
Handles are character strings that may consist of a wide range of characters. Every handle has two parts: its naming authority, followed by a unique local name under that authority, separated by the ASCII character /. The grammar gives the naming authority as one or more segments separated by the ASCII character ., where a segment is any octet that maps to a UTF-8 encoded Unicode character except the two octets for the period and the slash. The local name may be any octets that map to UTF-8 encoded Unicode characters.

Both parts are UTF-8 encoded, and the Handle System protocol mandates UTF-8 for handles transferred over the wire. The local name may use any character from the Unicode 2.0 standard. The naming authority may use any character except the slash, which is reserved as the separator.

Naming authorities are defined in a hierarchical fashion resembling a tree. Each node and leaf of the tree has a label that corresponds to a naming authority segment, and a naming authority is built by concatenating the labels from the root of the tree down to that node, with the labels separated by the period. The naming authority for the Digital Object Identifier project is 10, a root-level naming authority with no parent, and 10.1045 is a child of 10 for the D-Lib Magazine.

Handles are case sensitive by default. A handle service, global or local, may implement its namespace so that ASCII characters under it are treated as case insensitive, and the global handle service, the Global Handle Registry, does so. Because the Global Handle Registry manages the handles for all naming authorities, ASCII characters in naming authorities are treated as case insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: A handle has two halves: the authority that owns the name and the name itself, separated by a slash. The authority is a dotted path, so an organisation can sit under a larger authority and be given its own subtree of names.

sections.title: The Handle Value Set
sections.content:
Each handle may have a set of values assigned to it, and the Handle System maintains the value set and returns it in response to a resolution request. A handle value is a record of data fields. The index is an unsigned 32-bit integer that uniquely identifies the value within the set. The type is a UTF8-string, that is a four-byte unsigned integer followed by the character string, that identifies the data type defining the syntax and semantics of the data. The data field is a sequence of octets, preceded by its length in a four-byte unsigned integer, that describes the resource the handle identifies.

The permission field is an eight-bit bit-mask with six defined bits: PUBLIC_WRITE (0x01), PUBLIC_READ (0x02), ADMIN_WRITE (0x04), ADMIN_READ (0x08), PUBLIC_EXECUTE (0x10) and ADMIN_EXECUTE (0x20). A value with no read permission cannot leave the handle server, which makes it a place to store secret keys. A value with neither write permission is immutable and cannot be deleted through the protocol. Implementations may choose PUBLIC_READ and ADMIN_WRITE as the default, and handle servers must check permissions before fulfilling any client request.

The TTL field is an octet followed by a four-byte integer saying how long the record may be cached before the source is consulted again; a zero TTL means it is used only for the transaction in progress. The timestamp is an eight-byte integer recording the last update at the server, in milliseconds since 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970, chosen in milliseconds to avoid collisions when a value is updated. The reference field is a four-byte integer followed by a list of references to other handle values, which are generally used to add credentials to the current value, for example by referring to a digital signature issued by a commonly trusted entity.

By default the Handle System returns all the values with public-read permission in response to a resolution request, and a client may ask for a subset by data type or for one value by its index. Each value is uniquely referenced by the combination of the handle and its value index, so changing an index can break an existing reference. Index numbers need not be continuous and need not start at zero or one, as long as they are unique within the value set.
sections.plainLanguage: Each name holds a list of records. Every record says what kind of data it is, who may read it, who may change it, how long it may be cached, when it last changed and which other records vouch for it.

sections.title: Pre-defined Handle Data Types
sections.content:
Every handle value must have a data type, and the Handle System offers a registration service so that organisations can register types for their applications under the reserved naming authority 0.TYPE. The URL type, for example, is registered as the handle 0.TYPE/URL, and that handle may carry a value referring to the document that defines the syntax and semantics of a URL. Types may be hierarchical, with the period marking the boundary between levels, and a query may end with a period to ask for all the values under a hierarchy.

The system pre-defines a set of types to carry out the service itself. HS_ADMIN names the administrators of a handle: every handle must have at least one, each one holding a reference to a handle value that can be used to authenticate the administrator, and a 16-bit mask of administration privileges. The reference may hold a secret key, a public key or an X.509 certificate, and it may be the handle's own value, which lets a handle be administered without depending on any other handle. Naming authorities are themselves registered as handles under 0.NA, so 0.NA/10 is the naming authority handle for the naming authority 10, and only naming authority administrators can create handles or sub-naming authorities. The administrator permissions include Add_Handle (0x0001), Delete_Handle (0x0002), Add_NA (0x0004), Delete_NA (0x0008), Modify_Value (0x0010), Delete_Value (0x0020), Add_Value (0x0040), Modify_Admin (0x0080), Remove_Admin (0x0100) and Add_Admin (0x0200).

HS_SITE describes a service site: the server computers that make up the site, their addresses and their service configuration, including the port numbers and the service type. It carries a version number, a protocol version, a serial number that increases each time the value changes, a mask identifying the primary sites, the hash option used to spread handles among the servers, a list of attribute and value pairs for human explanations, and the list of server records. The hash options are HASH_BY_NA (0x00), HASH_BY_LOCAL (0x01) and HASH_BY_HANDLE (0x02), and the standard MD5 algorithm is used to spread handles among the servers.

HS_SERV points at a service handle, which is a name for a handle service, so that several naming authorities can share one set of site values and a change of configuration is made in one place. Service handles live under the reserved naming authority 0.SERV. HS_ALIAS makes one handle an alias for another, so a client that gets an alias value retries the query against the handle it names; the document suggests this as a way to transfer ownership of a resource without breaking references. HS_PRIMARY designates the primary service sites for a handle when the service has more than one. HS_VLIST makes a value a reference to a list of other values, which is how administrator groups are defined. HS_NA_DELEGATE supports the delegation of a naming authority to another party.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides the types organisations register for themselves, the system has fixed types for its own working: who administers a name, where a service site is, which site serves a name, another name for the same thing, and a list of values treated as one.

sections.title: The Service Model
sections.content:
The Handle System defines a hierarchical service model. At the top is the single distributed global handle service, the Global Handle Registry. Underneath it there can be any number of Local Handle Services, and each one must be registered with the Global Handle Registry to manage handles under a distinct set of naming authorities. The Global Handle Registry manages naming authorities through naming authority handles, and a naming authority handle also carries the service information, in the form of HS_SITE values, that describes the service responsible for handles under that authority. Clients use that information to choose a service site and find the responsible server.

The components are built to scale. A handle service may consist of multiple service sites that replicate one another, and each site may be a cluster of computers sharing the load, which avoids a single point of failure and lets weaker machines be used for the name service. A Local Handle Service manages handles under given sets of naming authorities, and each naming authority defines a local namespace of the handles under it. A naming authority is homed at a Local Handle Service when all its handles are managed there; a service may be home to several naming authorities, but a naming authority may be homed at only one. A Local Handle Service may also refer clients to another one, which distributes the service in a hierarchical fashion.

Between the clients and the service components sit the middle-ware components. A caching service reduces the traffic between clients and servers by holding handle data, including the service information of a Local Handle Service, and reusing what it got from earlier queries; it may take its data from a handle service or from another caching service. A proxy server lets handles be resolved over HTTP, so a handle can be resolved from a standard web browser without extra software, although a reference built that way then depends on the proxy server and breaks if its name changes. Neither caching nor proxy servers belong to any administration or authentication hierarchy: the Handle System protocol does not authenticate their responses, and clients are responsible for the trust relationship with the one they choose.
sections.plainLanguage: One global registry sits at the top and knows where everything else is. Below it, local services each look after their own set of names, and they can be spread over several sites and several machines. Between the client and the services, caching and proxy servers can sit to cut traffic or to let a browser do the lookup.

sections.title: Resolution and Authentication
sections.content:
Handle operations are either resolution or administration, and both may require the client to be authenticated. A client may send a request to any handle server; the response either answers the request or returns a status code that refers the request to another service component, asks for authentication, or signals an error. Any request must be directed to the home service of the handle, which the client finds by querying the corresponding naming authority handle against the Global Handle Registry, or from a local cache, or from its own configuration.

The resolution example in the document runs in four steps. The client asks the Global Handle Registry for the service information of the naming authority handle 0.NA/ncstrl.vatech_cs. The registry returns the service information for that naming authority. The client then queries the handle ncstrl.vatech_cs/tr-93-35 against the responsible handle server in the Local Handle Service, optionally authenticating itself first. The server returns the result, with a digital signature if the client asked for one, and the client verifies the signature with the public key from the service information. A session may be set up between a client and a server, identified by a session ID, and it may establish a session key used to authenticate or encrypt the messages exchanged within it.

For administration, the authentication protocol is a challenge-response. The server sends a challenge, a nonce plus an MD5 of the client request, and the client returns a reference to the handle administrator together with a challenge-response that proves possession of the administrator's secret, which may be a private key or a secret key. With a public key the response carries a digital signature that the server verifies; with a secret key it carries a message authentication code that the server recomputes and compares. The server then checks that the administrator has the required permission before it carries out the request.

The reference to the handle administrator, also called a key reference, may point at a value held by another handle server. In that case the server sends a verification request to that key server, carrying the challenge and the client's response, and the key server returns a signed verification response. The document warns that sharing a secret key this way is convenient but should not be used for highly sensitive handles, because the process is expensive, relies on a third party, and the key is open to dictionary attack since the key server cannot tell whether the verification request came from a legitimate server.

The security section adds that the security of the system depends on the handle administrator choosing and protecting their keys, that servers may set policy on key length and may prohibit secret keys, that execution permissions should be restricted to the account of the handle administrator, and that servers may enforce quotas on the number of handles under a naming authority, the number of values per handle, the maximum size of a value and the number of sub-naming authorities.
sections.plainLanguage: A client finds the right server by asking the global registry which service looks after that name. When it needs to change something, the server asks the client to prove who it is: it sends a random challenge, and the client signs it with the administrator's key. The server checks the signature and then checks what that administrator is allowed to do.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF A HANDLE VALUE

items.title: index
items.text: An unsigned 32-bit integer that identifies the value within the set of values for that handle.

items.title: type
items.text: A UTF8-string naming the data type that defines the syntax and meaning of the data.

items.title: data
items.text: A sequence of octets, with its length in a four-byte integer, describing the resource.

items.title: permission
items.text: An eight-bit mask saying who may read, write or execute the value.

items.title: TTL
items.text: How long the value may be cached before the source is consulted again; zero means do not cache.

items.title: timestamp
items.text: When the value was last updated at the server, in milliseconds since 1 January 1970.

items.title: reference
items.text: A list of references to other handle values, used to add credentials to this one.

viz.caption: THE PERMISSION BITS OF A HANDLE VALUE

items.label: PUBLIC_WRITE
items.desc: Lets anyone modify or delete the handle value.

items.label: PUBLIC_READ
items.desc: Lets anyone read the handle value.

items.label: ADMIN_WRITE
items.desc: Lets any handle administrator update or delete the value.

items.label: ADMIN_READ
items.desc: Lets a handle administrator with the right privilege read the value.

items.label: PUBLIC_EXECUTE
items.desc: Lets anyone run the program the value identifies, as an anonymous user.

items.label: ADMIN_EXECUTE
items.desc: Lets administrators run the program on the handle server, with their own privileges.
